passage: The power went out at nine, the night before Uday's first semester exam in Pune. He sat in the dark with his phone at four per cent, having just hung up on his mother in Guwahati. Her voice had made the flat feel even further from home. He hadn't told anyone he was homesick. Then there was a knock. Harsha, his flatmate, stood holding a candle and two steel tumblers of ginger tea. "Thought you might want this." Harsha didn't ask anything, just sat on the floor and started talking about the mess food. Uday laughed for the first time that day. When the lights came back an hour later, neither of them got up. Uday thought: this is someone I can count on.

qa.q: What did Harsha bring to Uday's room?
qa.a: A candle and two steel tumblers of ginger tea.

qa.q: How did Uday feel after hanging up on his mother?
qa.a: He felt homesick and lonely, as if the flat was even further from home.

qa.q: What was the turning point of Uday's night, and why did it help?
qa.a: Harsha's unasked visit with tea and easy talk turned a lonely evening into company, showing Uday he could count on someone here.

qa.q: What might Harsha have noticed that led to the knock?
qa.a: Harsha may have noticed Uday seemed low or heard the phone call end, and chose to offer company quietly without asking questions.

grounding: A homesick student receives tea and company from a flatmate without asking, and feels he belongs.

passage: It was Devika's third week in the Mumbai paying-guest flat, and Sunday was the worst day. At home in Mysuru, Sunday meant Amma's rasam, cousins, noise. Here there was just the fan and her laptop. She didn't cry; she just lay very still. Around four, Manjula, the flatmate she barely knew, tapped on the door with a tray: two cups of tea and a plate of hot bajji from the corner stall. "I saw you skipped lunch. Want to watch something silly?" They watched an old comedy on Manjula's laptop, knees up on the bed. Manjula didn't make a speech. She just came again next Sunday, and the one after. By the third week, Devika left her own door open on Sundays.

qa.q: What was on Manjula's tray?
qa.a: Two cups of tea and a plate of hot bajji from the corner stall.

qa.q: What does Devika lying very still suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt low and homesick, missing the noise and warmth of Sundays at home.

qa.q: What made Manjula's kindness so powerful for Devika?
qa.a: It came without being asked and kept coming every Sunday, so Devika learned she could rely on it and slowly opened her own door.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had only visited once?
qa.a: Devika might have felt a moment of comfort but not the steady sense of belonging that repeated Sundays gave her.

grounding: A homesick young woman is brought tea and time by a flatmate without asking and gradually feels she belongs.

passage: "You've been sitting on these steps for an hour." Chaitanya looked up. Pradeep, from the room next door in the hostel block, stood there holding two paper cups of canteen chai. "How did you know?" "Saw you from the window. Here." Chaitanya took the cup. "My grandmother called. Everyone's at home for the festival. I'm just... here." "Yeah." Pradeep sat down one step below. "Want to talk?" "Not really." "Okay." They drank. A crow hopped near. "Same time tomorrow?" Pradeep asked. Chaitanya looked at him. "You'd come again?" "Every day of the festival, if you want." Chaitanya felt something in his chest unknot. "Yeah. I'd like that."

qa.q: What was Pradeep holding when he came to the steps?
qa.a: Two paper cups of canteen chai.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya feel when his chest unknots?
qa.a: He feels relief and safety, sensing that someone cares about him while he is away from home during the festival.

qa.q: What choice made Pradeep's kindness work so well?
qa.a: Pradeep brought chai without being asked and accepted 'not really' without pushing, then offered to come every day, which made the care feel dependable.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's grandmother feel if she knew about Pradeep?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and comforted that someone was looking out for her grandson while the family celebrated without him.

grounding: A homesick student on the hostel steps receives unasked chai and quiet company from a fellow student and feels he belongs.

passage:
I'm Kashish, and looking back at my first month in Hyderabad, I remember how lost I felt. I'd come from Shillong, a skinny boy of eighteen, for my engineering course. The food was different, the heat was different, and at night the flat was so quiet I could hear my own homesickness.
I didn't tell anyone. But Sachin, my flatmate, must have noticed I'd stopped eating dinner. One night he knocked with two mugs of ginger tea and said, "Old cricket highlights?" He sat on my floor for an hour. He didn't ask what was wrong.
The next night he did it again. And the next. Once he brought a packet of chips from the only shop that stocked the kind we have back home.
By the end of that week, the flat didn't feel like a stranger's place anymore. I still missed home. But now there was a knock I could count on, and that made me feel I belonged there.

qa.q: What did Sachin bring on the first night?
qa.a: Two mugs of ginger tea.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel once Sachin's knock became a nightly thing?
qa.a: He felt safer and less alone; the flat stopped feeling like a stranger's place, and he felt he belonged there.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's choices mattered most to Kashish, and why?
qa.a: Coming back every night without asking what was wrong mattered most, because the steady small kindness showed Kashish he could count on someone.

qa.q: How might Sachin have seen Kashish during that first month?
qa.a: Sachin probably noticed a quiet flatmate who had stopped eating and guessed he was struggling, choosing company over questions.

grounding: It shows a homesick student whose flatmate brings tea and time every night without being asked, and who comes to feel safe and that he belongs.

passage:
Warden's note, girls' hostel, Friday. Mrs Rathore.
Kalyani (first year, from Thrissur) has been quiet since she arrived in Jaipur. She skipped dinner twice and told me the food "tastes like nowhere." I noticed her eyes were often red in the mornings.
This week, something changed. Her roommate Ritu has been bringing two cups of tea to their room every evening at seven, without being asked, and they sit on the balcony. On Wednesday I saw Ritu teaching her a card game in the common room, and Kalyani laughing.
When I asked Kalyani how she was, she said, "Still miss home, ma'am. But now there's someone here who notices." She said it simply, almost surprised.
Next: I will keep an eye on Kalyani, and I will tell Ritu quietly that what she is doing matters.

qa.q: What time does Ritu bring tea every evening?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What does Kalyani's answer, 'now there's someone here who notices,' show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she still misses home but now feels safe and cared for, because someone in the hostel pays attention to her.

qa.q: What choice by Ritu made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Bringing tea every evening without being asked, and teaching her a card game, gave Kalyani dependable small kindness that told her she belonged.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when the warden tells her that what she is doing matters?
qa.a: Ritu might feel surprised and pleased, since she was simply being kind and may not have known how much it helped.

grounding: It shows a homesick student who is brought tea and time by her roommate without asking, and who begins to feel safe and that she belongs.

passage:
Tuesday night
Today was bad. Onam at home, and I'm here in a Delhi flat, with a lab report due. Amma sent a photo of the sadya on the banana leaf. I stared at it for ages. Then I lay on my bed and didn't move.
At six, there was a knock. Neelam, with two cups of tea and a packet of banana chips from somewhere. "I read it was Onam," she said. "I don't know how to make sadya. But I brought chips."
She didn't ask me to talk. She just sat on the floor and drank her tea. After a while I told her about the pookalam my cousins make, and she listened like it was the most interesting thing in the world.
When she left I felt like I belonged somewhere again.
– Preeti

qa.q: What did Neelam bring besides tea?
qa.a: A packet of banana chips.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel after Neelam left?
qa.a: Preeti felt safe and cared for, as if belonging somewhere again.

qa.q: Why did Neelam's quiet visit help so much?
qa.a: She came without being asked, sat with tea and listened, which showed Preeti through a small, dependable kindness that someone cared.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel after the visit?
qa.a: She might feel glad and a little closer to Preeti, having learned about the pookalam.

grounding: It shows a homesick student feeling safe and cared for when a flatmate brings tea and time unasked.

passage:
Indu and her younger brother Sahil rented one small room in Dharwad while they studied at the college there, hours from their village. Sahil, eighteen, had been quiet all week. It was the first harvest he had missed.
On Sunday Indu came back from the market with a packet of jaggery and a newspaper cone of roasted groundnuts, the kind their father sold at the fair.
She made two glasses of strong tea, put the groundnuts between them and sat on the floor beside his mat.
"Tell me what Appa's doing today," she said.
Sahil talked for an hour: the threshing, the bullocks, their mother's loud singing. Indu mostly listened, cracking shells.
That night Sahil said, "I thought nobody here noticed." He slept well for the first time in days.

qa.q: What did Indu bring back from the market?
qa.a: A packet of jaggery and a newspaper cone of roasted groundnuts.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he said "I thought nobody here noticed"?
qa.a: He felt surprised and relieved, finally cared for after a lonely, homesick week.

qa.q: What made Indu's kindness work?
qa.a: She noticed without being told, brought something familiar and gave him time to talk, making him feel he belonged.

qa.q: How might Indu feel hearing what Sahil said?
qa.a: She would probably feel glad and a little sad, realising how lonely he had been.

grounding: It shows a homesick student feeling cared for when the person he lives with brings tea and time unasked.

passage:
Sofia had been in Dublin for three weeks and still hadn't unpacked her last suitcase. That Sunday she sat on her bed, scrolling photos of her family's lunch in Lisbon, feeling the ache in her throat.
There was a knock. Her flatmate Layla stood there with two mugs of tea and a packet of biscuits.
"I heard your door close really softly," Layla said. "That's usually a sad sign. Want company?"
Sofia hadn't said a word to anyone. She laughed and cried at the same time.
Layla sat on the floor, and they looked at photos together. Layla asked about each face.
Later, alone again, Sofia unpacked the last suitcase. For the first time, the room felt like it might become home.

qa.q: What did Layla bring to Sofia's door?
qa.a: She brought two mugs of tea and a packet of biscuits.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel when Layla offered company without being asked?
qa.a: She felt touched and relieved, laughing and crying at once, because someone noticed her homesickness.

qa.q: What does Layla's small act show about how to help a homesick friend?
qa.a: Noticing quiet signs and simply showing up with tea and time can make someone feel they belong.

qa.q: What might it be like for Layla to sit and hear about Sofia's family?
qa.a: Layla might enjoy it and feel closer to Sofia, glad her small gesture helped.

grounding: A homesick student receives tea and time from a flatmate without asking and begins to feel she belongs.

passage:
Harsha's first semester in the engineering hostel in Nagpur was rough. The food didn't taste like home, and he missed his mother's voice so much he stopped calling, because the calls made it worse.
One evening, his roommate Gurpreet came back from the canteen with two cups of cutting chai and put one beside Harsha's books.
"You've been quiet since Tuesday."
Harsha hadn't told anyone anything. He stared at the tea.
"No need to talk," Gurpreet said. "I'll just sit here."
He sat on the other bed and studied. Every evening that week, the tea appeared at the same time.
By Friday Harsha told him about his town and his mother's lemon pickle. Then he called home. He felt, finally, that someone here had his back.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet bring back from the canteen?
qa.a: He brought two cups of cutting chai.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when the tea kept appearing every evening?
qa.a: He felt cared for and safe, as if someone here had his back, which eased his homesickness.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's help work?
qa.a: It was small, steady and without pressure: tea every evening and quiet company, which told Harsha he belonged.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Harsha finally talks about his town?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably feels glad and closer to him, seeing the quiet care had helped.

passage:
Dear Amma,
Don't worry, I'm okay now. I want to tell you something that happened.
Last week I was so homesick I couldn't eat. I missed your sambar, our Chennai sea breeze, even our neighbour's loud TV. I didn't tell anyone here in Delhi.
But my flatmate Anjali noticed. She didn't ask questions. She just made me ginger tea every night and sat on my bed while I studied. On Saturday she took me to a South Indian place near the metro, "so you can argue about the chutney."
Amma, I felt safe for the first time since I got here. It's small, but it tells me I'm not alone.
I'll call you Sunday.
Keerthana

qa.q: What did Anjali make every night?
qa.a: She made ginger tea every night.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after Anjali's care?
qa.a: Keerthana felt safe and less alone for the first time since arriving, cared for without having asked.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do to return Anjali's kindness?
qa.a: Thank her, share some home food or stories, and look out for her in small ways when she needs it.

qa.q: How might Amma feel reading this letter?

passage: So you want to know when Pune started feeling like home? Honestly, it was a Tuesday in my second month here. My name's Kunal, by the way, and back then I was a mess. I'd called home, heard the pressure cooker whistle in our kitchen in Nagpur, and after hanging up I just sat on my bed staring at the wall. My flatmate Hemant knocked, didn't ask anything, and put a steel glass of ginger chai on my desk. Then he sat on the floor and complained about his lab partner, loudly, for about an hour. I laughed twice. He did the same thing the next Tuesday, and the one after. I never asked him to. I think that's the point: he just kept turning up, so I stopped feeling like a guest in my own life.

qa.q: What did Hemant put on Kunal's desk?
qa.a: A steel glass of ginger chai.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling after hanging up the call home?
qa.a: Kunal felt homesick and low, sitting on the bed staring at the wall after hearing the pressure cooker whistle back home.

qa.q: What makes Hemant's way of helping work so well?
qa.a: It asks nothing of Kunal: Hemant brings chai, fills the silence and comes back each week, so the care feels steady rather than a one-time rescue.

qa.q: How might Hemant see those Tuesday evenings?
qa.a: Hemant may see them as ordinary time with a flatmate rather than a big favour, which is partly why Kunal found them easy to accept.

grounding: A homesick student describes a flatmate's unasked, repeated chai visits making the city feel like home.

passage:
Monday, week one: Vikas ate dinner alone in his room in the Chennai flat, a packet of biscuits and a photo of the tea garden behind his house in Assam. The ceiling fan was loud. He did not go out when he heard Abhinav's music in the hall.
Thursday: a knock. Abhinav stood there with two cups of lemon tea. 'I made too much. Also, I'm bad at being alone.' He stayed till midnight, asking about the hills, the rain, Vikas's grandmother's pickles.
Two Sundays later: nobody had asked, but the tea kept arriving, Thursdays and sometimes Mondays. When his mother called, Vikas said, 'Wait, Ma, my flatmate is shouting about rice,' and heard himself laughing. He did not reach for the photo that night.

qa.q: What did Abhinav bring on Thursday?
qa.a: Abhinav brought two cups of lemon tea.

qa.q: What had changed in how Vikas felt by the third beat?
qa.a: Vikas felt settled and more at home; laughing on the call and not reaching for the photo show the homesick loneliness had eased.

qa.q: What small step could Vikas take now to keep this bond steady?
qa.a: He could return the kindness his own way, perhaps sharing the grandmother's pickles with Abhinav, so the care flows both ways.

qa.q: What might Abhinav gain from these evenings?
qa.a: Abhinav admitted being bad at being alone, so the tea visits probably ease his own loneliness too, not only Vikas's.

grounding: Over two weeks a lonely student is brought tea and company unasked and begins to feel he belongs.

passage: You're packing for Bengaluru, Sahil, so let me tell you something your Usha Maasi never told anyone. My first year in Delhi, I cried into my pillow every night so the other girls in the hostel wouldn't hear. The food tasted of nothing. Then Onam came, and I couldn't go home; the train ticket was more than I had. That evening Parveen, my roommate, the loud one from Lucknow, came in with two cups of tea and a banana leaf she had begged from the mess. 'I don't know how to make your sadya,' she said, 'but I brought rice and I brought me.' We sat on the floor and ate with our hands. She never made a speech about it. She just came back every night that week with tea. That's when the room became my room, beta.

qa.q: What did Parveen bring on Onam evening?
qa.a: Two cups of tea and a banana leaf she had begged from the mess.

qa.q: How did Usha feel before that Onam evening, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt deeply homesick and lonely; she cried into her pillow every night and said the food tasted of nothing.

qa.q: Parveen brought rice and herself instead of trying to cook a proper sadya. Why did that choice work?
qa.a: It showed she cared without pretending to fix everything; her plain, repeated company told Usha she belonged, which a perfect meal alone could not.

qa.q: How might Parveen have seen that evening?
qa.a: Parveen probably saw it as a small, natural thing to do for a roommate far from home, which is why she never made a speech about it.

grounding: An aunt recalls a hostel roommate who brought tea and company unasked, making her feel safe far from home.

passage:
It was Karva Chauth, and back in Jaipur Mummy would be on the terrace with the other aunties, sieve in hand, waiting for the moon. In the Bengaluru flat the power had gone at eight, and Mahima sat on the balcony in the dark, scrolling family photos until her battery hit nine percent. She hadn't told anyone she was sad.
The door creaked. Samir came out with two steel glasses of masala tea and a candle stuck on a saucer.
"You didn't eat dinner," he said, handing her one. He sat on the step beside her and didn't ask anything.
They watched the sky for a while. When the moon finally slid out from behind the clouds, Mahima laughed, a little shakily. "Mummy can eat now."
"Then so can you," Samir said, and passed her a packet of biscuits.

qa.q: What did Samir bring out to the balcony?
qa.a: Two steel glasses of masala tea and a candle stuck on a saucer.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel when Samir sits beside her without asking anything?
qa.a: Mahima, homesick and alone in the dark, likely feels comforted and safe, cared for without having to explain.

qa.q: What made Samir's kindness work so well?
qa.a: He noticed she had skipped dinner, came without being asked, and sat quietly instead of questioning her, letting her share the moment in her own time.

qa.q: What might Samir have noticed that evening?
qa.a: Samir probably noticed that Mahima had skipped dinner and was sitting alone on the balcony, and guessed she was missing home.

grounding: A homesick student on a festival night is brought tea and quiet company by a flatmate and feels she belongs.
